Netflix Is Searching For Its Next Big Story. The Protagonist? Itself

Netflix Is Searching For Its Next Big Story. The Protagonist? Itself
articles.content: Netflix is in the storytelling business, but it seems to have lost the plot on perhaps the most interesting story it needs to be telling: Its own. That may be at the heart of the stunning shake up at the company over the last week, which saw content chief Bela Bejaria, film head Dan Lin and 1,000 or so other employees let go in a plan to refocus the company’s content under new hire Peter Rice. To understand what’s going on requires you to understand Netflix’s unique (at least for the media business) ability to tell its story to Wall Street, and to do so in a way that valued the company as though it were a tech titan like Google or Apple. Netflix was once part of the legendary group of FAANG stocks that drove stock market growth for years. Once it began its pursuit of Warner Bros. last year, however, Wall Street got spooked. All of sudden Netflix is being valued more like a traditional media company, rather than a high-flying tech company. All of a sudden, a company that was so good at selling its story , through subscriber numbers, through selective drops of viewership data, through its consistent and growing revenues and profits, created its own plot twist. The WB deal sent a message to Wall Street (a prescient one, it turns out, given the last week’s news) that something may have been amiss with its content. Why else would Netflix so fully be willing to embrace theatrical movies or be willing to take on linear assets like HBO or TCM? And Netflix embarked on a series of bets that appear to have not paid off, not paid off as much as expected, or that are still in the development phase. Some of those bets are sure to stick around (the advertising tier, live events) but others are less certain (podcasts, gaming, creator deals, Netflix House experiences). articles.content: Filming in Los Angeles is continuing to slide despite California’s urgent bid to revive production in the region. L.A. saw a nearly 5 percent drop in shoot days from June to September compared to the same period last year and an 11 percent drop compared to the previous quarter, according to the latest report from permitting office FilmLA issued on Wednesday. The total is 36 percent below the five-year average, highlighting the fierce competition between states and other countries to host Hollywood. The decline comes despite California’s expansion of its film and television tax credit last year, which increased the program’s annual funding from $330 million to $750 million and broadened eligibility to additional types of productions. Projects getting subsidies to shoot in the state accounted for a record 40 percent of on-location filming in L.A.. Since July 2025, 214 projects have been tapped to receive tax incentives under the expanded program, according to the commission. While the credits are luring individual productions to California — like Tracker, which moved from Canada to L.A. for its fourth season — the latest figures suggest that it hasn’t reversed the region’s production downturn. “Overall production remains far below where Los Angeles needs it to be, and crews and businesses across the region are feeling it,” said FilmLA CEO Denise Gutches. Shooting for TV shows, a key source of work for L.A. crews, recorded 1,400 shoot days in the quarter, down roughly three percent from a year earlier. Drama production fell nine percent, to 494 shoot days, even as the number of days logged by dramas getting incentives more than doubled. Comedy production rose sharply, increasing 143 percent to 192 shoot days, with nearly all of the growth coming from productions receiving tax credits. The project landed at Paramount+ in a competitive situation involving multiple bidders. It is the streamer’s first known major buy in the genre/sci-fi/world-building arena. In Zero Hour, written by Carnahan, when mysterious ovals appear in the sky, the world changes forever. articles.content: James Talarico is decidedly not running for Senate in California. But Ken Paxton wants you to think he is. “California already has two senators. If elected, James Talarico would be California’s third senator,” Talarico’s opponent for Texas’ open Senate seat recently told Newsweek . The attack comes as Hollywood donors line up behind the 37-year-old Democratic populist. Peter Chernin and Damon Lindelof have hosted fundraisers for Talarico; Robert De Niro headlined a New York fundraiser; and Brad Garrett, Holland Taylor and Noah Wyle have all kicked in dollars to help Texas elect a Democratic senator for the first time since 1988. Support from some of America’s best-known entertainers might seem like an asset. But this election season, Hollywood is a gun Republicans are trying to turn against their opponents. As the midterms come into the heated homestretch ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3, Republicans have found what they hope is a potent new avenue, especially in the South and Midwest: knock a candidate’s celebrity connections. They hope it can stop what many polls say will be a blue wave, even as it’s unclear that voters in a time of costs and crisis care which sitcom star might vote for you. Running against “the media” has been a time-tested strategy to get GOP candidates elected, no matter that Fox News is the most watched cable channel in the country. But after a 2024 election season when the support of Beyoncé, Eminem and Taylor Swift didn’t help Kamala Harris and in some swing states may have hurt her, GOP strategists and pundits nationwide are doubling down on a newer anti-celebrity gambit. articles.summary: Exclusive: One of the most expensive films ever produced in Japan, the '90s Christmas feature had its theatrical release cut short after its director was arrested for cocaine smuggling.
articles.content: Kani Releasing will bring the 1993 feature “Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story” stateside in December, setting its first-ever U.S. theatrical release. The Christmas-set comedy, which features animatronics by Italian effects guru and “E.T. the Extra Terrestrial” design creator Carlo Rambaldi, will receive a one-week run at New York’s independent theater Metrograph on December 11, with openings in Chicago, Seattle, Austin, and other markets to follow. Released in Japan on July 3, 1993, “Rex” was heavily marketed and positioned to contend with the ranks of rival U.S. tentpoles. The blockbuster ambitions are best illustrated by the production’s recruitment of Rambaldi. The effects artist began his career in the Italian film industry, working filmmakers like Dario Argento and Mario Bava, before making a jump to Hollywood and contributing to productions like “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” “Alien,” and “Dune.” “Rex” was certainly chasing the child-actor and animatronic two-hander dramatics of “E.T.,” which were made possible by Rambaldi’s work designing the character . But at a production budget of 2 billion yen, the family film was still a money loser in theaters. As Kani Releasing describes it, original distributor Shochiku also pulled “Rex” from theaters after the film’s then-dominant director Haruki Kadokawa was accused of instructing an aide to smuggle cocaine from the United States. Though the blockbuster director argued his innocence, he was convicted in 1994 and served a two-and-a-half year sentence. articles.summary: Over 30 percent of young people feel either "doomed" or "scared" when watching AI-generated content, but a study found notable differences in age groups.
articles.content: One of the more inexplicably popular sources of AI slop today is “Fruit Love Island,” an AI -generated TikTok parody series in which anthropomorphized fruits with abs and cleavage flirt and mingle in 60-second ripoffs of “Love Island.” It is as mind-numbingly dumb as it sounds, and though TikTok started suppressing and demonetizing the videos due to being low quality AI, per the series’ own website blog posts, it persists and has tens of millions of views. Suffice it to say, your teenager or pre-teen may very well have come across these videos or could easily be obsessed with them. But depending on just how old your teen is, their mileage may vary. articles.title: Q3 earnings
articles.content: Battered Netflix shares tumbled in after-hours trading Tuesday as the company lowered full-year advertising guidance and issued an updated revenue outlook that disappointed Wall Street. The swoon came despite a solid set of financials for the third quarter. Earnings per share of 87 cents beat Wall Street expectations, rising from 59 cents in the same period of 2025. Revenue of $12.87 billion, up 12% year-over-year, matched the Street estimate. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise 12% to $13.4 billion, while full-year revenue is now projected to come in at $51.1 billion. While that would be 13% above 2025 levels, the new forecast is slightly below analysts’ consensus and also at the low end of the range the company provided in prior earnings reports. Higher expenses, meanwhile, including those related to the recent layoff of about 1,000 workers , will also squeeze operating margins. Watch on Deadline Advertising revenue is now projected to be $2.7 billion for 2026, compared with earlier forecasts for $3 billion. In its quarterly letter to shareholders, the company blamed the reduction on “slightly slower than expected rollout of some ad product capabilities.” The results come on the heels of last week’s layoffs , the company’s deepest cuts since 2022, as well as the ouster of high-level executives including content chief Bela Bajaria . articles.title: ‘Paper Tiger’ Producer Rodrigo Teixeira Set for GLAFF’s First Visionary Award, Presented by Wagner Moura (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.content: Two-time Oscar-nominated producer Rodrigo Teixeira will receive the inaugural Árbol de la Vida Visionary Award at the GuadaLAjara Film Festival (GLAFF), the Los Angeles offshoot of the Guadalajara International Film Festival, on Nov. 6. articles.content: Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones have thrown their support behind Sally Rooney , whose book “Normal People” would catapult them both to fame following its hit TV adaptation. She first arrived on the big screen in 1997’s “Batman & Robin” and was played by Uma Thurman. In live-action TV, she also appeared in “Gotham” and “Batwoman,” and she’s popped up in several animated shows like “Batman: The Brave and the Bold,” “The New Batman Adventures,” “Young Justice” and more. articles.title: Neon Will Distribute ‘NAZA,’ Providing a Major Boost and Seal of Approval
articles.summary: The Oscar-decorated studio is now behind the Gaza whistleblower doc
articles.content: NAZA just won a powerful U.S. film ally as it seeks to continue its box office momentum. Neon is coming aboard to distribute Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary about the Israeli military in Gaza, with the Oscar-decorated studio rolling out the movie to theaters from this point forward. The company will provide publicity support, theater booking, P&A funds and other resources as it does for all its acquisitions, according to sources. The decision by one of the most well-regarded studios operating today to acquire rights to NAZA provides the whistleblowing doc with a strong artistic seal-of-approval. It also financially supercharged what has already been a robust independent release . NAZA has taken in nearly $900,000 in less than two weeks in North American theaters, adding to its total of more than $6.5 million overseas. Neon said in a statement that it “will work with the filmmakers to expand its footprint and to reach larger audiences and communities.” The movie had not to date had a traditional distributor, with the producing entities — they include The Guardian and international-sales company MK2 — putting it into theaters themselves. Neon reps say they have been talking to the people behind the film (they also include director Jonathan Glazer and his producing partner James Wilson) about a potential deal since an enthusiastic New York Film Festival screening last month. In the documentary, Abraham interviews some two dozen IDF soldiers involved in Israel’s war in Gaza, building off pieces he did for The Guardian and other publications. The filmmaker speaks to the soldiers anonymously and in shadow on Tel Aviv rooftops, with the whistleblowers documenting in specific and often chilling detail how they personally conducted the war that began in the fall of 2023 after Hamas attacked communities in southern Israel. Denis Villeneuve ‘s hotly anticipated sci-fi sequel raked in £880,000 ($1.2m) in presales, compared to the £750,000 ($1m) Christopher Nolan’s three-hour epic recently scored. In third place is 2024’s Dune: Part Two , which comes in at less than half of The Odyssey ‘s tally (£366k). Behind that is Oppenheimer (£254k) and Avatar: Fire and Ash (£116k). Wednesday’s figures follow three opening weekend screenings that had previously sold out in under an hour last April and two previews that also sold out earlier this month. The British Film Institute (BFI) is presenting Villeneuve’s final Dune outing on a “pristine” IMAX 70mm print, “continuing the organization’s commitment to preserving and celebrating celluloid, alongside the filmmakers who champion the format.” Related Stories Movies John C. articles.title: John C. Reilly, Penny Lane Board Short Doc ‘Stalin Boys’ as Executive Producers (Exclusive)
articles.summary: Reilly hopes the short film will remind people "that big lives always start small, and even tiny dusty towns in the middle of nowhere can produce people who can shape a brighter future for us all."
articles.content: Nonfiction filmmaker Penny Lane ( Confessions of a Good Samaritan ) and Academy Award-nominated actor John C. Reilly have boarded the short documentary film Stalin Boys as executive producers. Directed by Ora DeKornfeld and Bianca Giaever, the film follows Malachi, a middle school student in Marathon, Texas, who is obsessed with Joseph Stalin . Yes, THAT Joseph Stalin! When he hears about the Texas History Day competition, he writes a play about the late Soviet dictator and enlists his friends Cayden, Lyric and Jurem to play fearful civilians and loyal henchmen. The film debuted on The New York Times Op-Docs earlier this month and is eligible for the Academy Award for Documentary Short Film category. articles.title: “Horror Is Now Cool” as the Hunt for the Next ‘Obsession’ and ‘Backrooms’ Is on: Rome’s MIA
articles.summary: "We want to find the Italian Kane Parsons" to reach Gen Z audiences, a genre film panel discussing the state of the medium at the MIA Market heard on Wednesday.
articles.content: Horror industry leaders came to Rome to praise Curry Barker and Kane Parsons — the YouTubers-turned-directors behind the breakout Obsession and Backrooms horror movies. “The stigma of horror of the past, that it was niche, is past. Horror is now cool, and that’s great,” Andrea Romeo, founder and CEO of Wonder Pictures, which released Backrooms in Italy, told a panel on the genre at the MIA Market in Rome. Peter Kuplowsky, programmer of the Toronto Film Festival’s thrills and spills Midnight Madness showcase, said the Hollywood box office rebound has helped underpin the resurgence in horror films. articles.title: Hiam Abbass to Receive European Achievement in World Cinema Award
articles.summary: The Palestinian actress, whose credits include 'Paradise Now,' 'The Visitor,' 'Succession' and  'Palestine 36,' will be honored at the 39th European Film Awards in Athens in January.
articles.content: Hiam Abbass will be honored with the 2027 European Achievement in World Cinema Award. The acclaimed Palestinian actress will receive the honor “for her astounding body of work” at the 39th European Film Awards in Athens in January. Abbass has been a figure on the European film scene at least since her first lead role in 1989 in Ariane Mnouchkine’s La Nuit Miraculeuse . She has since appeared in more than 100 films across Palestinian, Arab and international productions, in such features as Paradise Now by Hany Abu-Assad, Tom McCarthy’s The Visitor , The Limits of Control by Jim Jarmusch, Julian Schnabel’s Miral , Blade Runner 2049 by Denis Villeneuv, Gaza Mon Amour by Arab and Tarzan Nasser, and Palestine 36 by Annemarie Jacir. Her latest, Atonement , from Reed Van Dyk, premiered in Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight. She received a People’s Choice Award nomination in 2005 for The Syrian Bride and a European Actress nomination in 2008 for Lemon Tree , which also earned her an Asia Pacific Screen Award. Born in Nazareth to a Palestinian family forced into exile in 1948, Abbass began her acting career at the Palestinian National Theatre El-Hakawati in East Jerusalem, which Israeli authorities frequently closed. During a theater tour of Europe, she decided to leave Palestine for London. She has lived in Paris since the late 1980s. Abbass’ performance in In Syria by Philippe Van Leeuw earned a nomination at the French Lumière Awards in 2018. On television, she appeared in the Hulu series Ramy and as Marcia Roy, the wife of Brian Cox’s Logan Roy, in the HBO series Succession , for which she received a Primetime Emmy nomination in 2023. articles.content: Batman adversary and Gotham’s biggest plant lover, Poison Ivy, may be getting her own television series. The Penguin creator and showrunner Lauren LeFranc is in talks to produce a series on the super-villain for HBO and DC Studios , The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed. articles.title: What Happened to Natalee Holloway? Netflix’s ‘Taken’ Documentary Trailer Revisits the Case
articles.summary: Netflix's latest true-crime documentary looks back at Holloway's tragic disappearance.
articles.content: Netflix is revisiting the tragic case of Natalee Holloway, an 18-year-old who vanished on a high school graduation trip to Aruba in 2005. The three-part documentary Taken: Natalee Holloway released its first trailer (below). The project, from Story Syndicate ( Titan: The OceanGate Disaster ) and directors Dani Sloane and Matthew Galkin, is described as “the definitive account of a case that gripped a nation.” “Growing up in the mid-2000s, it was impossible to turn on the TV or walk by a newsstand without seeing Natalee Holloway’s face,” Sloane said. “But, beyond the wall-to-wall coverage and sensational headlines, is a story about the incredible courage, devotion, and strength that Natalee’s mother, Beth, showed in the face of unimaginable loss. For me, as a mother and filmmaker, Beth’s steadfastness and dedication to her daughter is nothing short of inspiring, and I’m so proud to be able to share her story.” Related Stories Business Netflix Stock and Price Targets Drop as Wall Street Debates If the Streamer Can Flip the Script Business Netflix: "We Need Better Execution" in U.S., and Peter Rice Can Deliver It From the official description: “On May 30, 2005, 18-year-old Natalee Holloway vanished on a high school graduation trip to Aruba — and never came home. What followed was years of unanswered questions, a missing teenager, and a mother’s relentless fight for the truth. Now, over 20 years later, Natalee’s mother, Beth, is ready to tell the complete story — with exclusive, unprecedented access to Beth and those who were with Natalee when she vanished … This is Natalee’s story, told at last in full.” In 2023, Joran van der Sloot, the Dutch man who was the last person seen with Holloway before her disappearance, confessed to killing her.

articles.title: How Lucille Ball Saved ‘Star Trek’ to Become a Six-Decade Juggernaut Franchise
articles.summary: Roddenberry Entertainment COO Trevor Roth on Wednesday told the MIA Market in Rome how the comedy legend and her Desilu Productions put the quirky sci-fi series into reruns after an NBC cancellation.
articles.content: Roddenberry Entertainment COO Trevor Roth on Wednesday paid tribute to an unlikely savior for the original Star Trek TV series: Lucille Ball . “ Star Trek was a failed television series for a very long time. It did not do well, and by the stars aligning, it found its way into the hearts and minds of audiences in the United States and around the world,” Roth told the MIA Market in Rome. One star to save the series created by the late Gene Roddenberry was comedy legend Ball, who after NBC canceled the original series had seen how husband Desi Arnaz and his Desilu Productions put the iconic I Love Lucy comedy series into reruns. Roddenberry Entertainment was founded by Gene Roddenberry, with his son, Rod Roddenberry, today serving as CEO. The Star Trek series originally hit the air in 1966 and has since sustained a Trekkie fan base. articles.title: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Two Married Couples Begin to Covet Each Others’ Lives in the Latest Stunner from ‘Burning’ Director Lee Chang-dong
articles.summary: Class conflict achieves vivid new dimension in this sprawling Netflix drama about the relationship between a rich documentary filmmaker and her blue collar subjects.
articles.content: [Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 6, 2026 at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Netflix will release “ Possible Love ” in theaters on Friday, October 23 before it streams beginning on November 6.] Another heart-stopping and novelistically layered stunner from modern cinema’s most literary auteur (a fiction author himself), Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love” might be dedicated to the memory of Krzysztof Kieślowski’s “Dekalog 10,” but let’s dispel any notion of it being a remake. articles.title: ‘Clayface’ Review: A Gross Miscalculation (Emphasis on the Gross)
articles.summary: James Watkins' gory, goopy R-rated body horror is an offbeat addition to the DCU's increasingly erratic output, but it feels much more like a curiosity than an essential story.
articles.content: Three films into its latest “chapter” (this one subtitled “Gods and Monsters”), James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DCU can’t be faulted for making interesting choices. Hell, at least they’re making choices at all. Kicking off their incarnation of the latest run of comic book movies with “Superman” was unquestionably smart (it’s Superman! you know him!), even if its follow-up “Supergirl” was destined to divide audiences (even if this critic quite liked it, surely there are other reasons why some members of this seemingly dedicated audience didn’t, no matter its quality). Enter: “Clayface.” Another set of execs and filmmakers wouldn’t have bellied up to this grim, gross anti-hero to round out their first trio of movies meant to reset a massive franchise. But does that kind of ambition and vision pay off in James Watkins ‘ goopy, gory, decidedly R-rated body horror feature? Not so much, even as open-minded audiences will likely admire the big swings on offer here. It’s certainly different , and for comic book movie fans absolutely bored to death by the same old stuff , it’s something of a respite. Yet, divorced from all that, Watkins’ film confounds much more than it compels. articles.title: Tom Cruise to Be Honored with AFI Life Achievement Award
articles.summary: The "Digger" and "Mission: Impossible" star will be at the center of a gala tribute in Los Angeles in April.
articles.content: Tom Cruise will be the 52nd recipient of the American Film Institute ‘s prestigious life achievement award. articles.title: Watch Ava Duvernay Explain Why the 14th Amendment Is So Much More Than Birthright Citizenship
articles.summary: At IndieWire's Art of the Doc event, the "13th" director explained why her Netflix follow-up contained much more than she initially expected.
articles.content: When Ava DuVernay approached Netflix about making a follow-up to “13th,” her acclaimed documentary about the legacy of the constitutional amendment that abolished slavery, she thought it was a fairly straightforward proposition. The 14th Amendment is best known for offering U.S. citizenship to everyone born in America, a right that is frequently attacked by the current administration. That seemed like enough material for another film , but the two-year process of making “14th” taught her that the amendment contains so much more. During a conversation with IndieWire’s Chris O’Falt at our Art of the Doc event in Los Angeles, DuVernay explained how the project evolved over time. The parts where I was like ‘This is too hard, I don’t want to focus on these other parts.’ But when we started to hear them coming up in those headlines, you couldn’t leave that out.” The duo discussed how the constitutional amendment “flies under the radar” compared to more notable ones that everyone memorizes in history class, despite containing important protections like the Equal Protection Clause and the Due Process Clause. “It does [fly under the radar],” she said. “Which is wild, because it holds in it the rights that we abide by.I didn’t realize the depth that was in the 14th amendment. articles.title: ‘Sinner Supper Club,’ a Gay Mumblegore Ghost Story, Sells to Factory 25
articles.summary: Shot in six days on an iPhone, the film will premiere at NewFest.
articles.content: Factory 25 , a Brooklyn-based independent film distribution company, has acquired worldwide rights to Daisy Rosato and Nora Kaye’s first feature film “Sinner Supper Club” at the New York premiere of the film at NewFest . The film is described as a “gay mumblegore ghost story” about friends reuniting to throw a “wake” for Genevieve, who has been priced out of New York City. As the night progresses and a heatwave traps them together, their long-ignored problems boil over….and then their dead friend shows up. The film was shot in six days on an iPhone through improvisation. It is an homage to the scrappy and experimental filmmaking that characterized both the mumblegore and Dogme 95 movements. As part of production, the filmmakers wrote a manifesto, one that explored what it means to make a film in the 2020’s, with characters that represent the queer and transgender and gender nonconforming community. Related Stories Nathan Fielder Was Not Supposed to Be in ‘You Can See Everything’ $1 Million Box Office Haul for ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ Provides a Release Template for the Smallest of Indies The cast includes Elise Kibler, Ashil Lee, Genevieve Simon, Jayae Riley Jr., Sophie Sagan-Gutherz, Kaye and Rosato. In addition to directing and appearing in the film, Kaye and Rosato wrote the screenplay. Rosato also served as the cinematographer. Factory 25 is planning a spring 2027 theatrical release followed by a digital and Blu-ray release. Factory 25 has released such films as “Funny Ha Ha,” “Ham on Rye,” “Happer’s Comet,” “Actual People,” “This Closeness,” “Family Portrait,” and “Queens of the Qing Dynasty.” NewFest was founded in 1988 in response to the AIDS crisis. The New York LGBTQ+ Film Festival has been a tentpole of NYC’s queer cultural scene. In the subsequent years, NewFest has expanded into a film and media organization with year-long programs to serve all facets of the LGBTQ+ community.
